items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: or maybe Joe Temperly. They come out of a different sort of school which is in a kind of the swing-bebop thing

ctx.x: These situations at the jazz festivals where you have three or four horns on stage and you pick a standard, is it that much different from the New Orleans jazz, as far as how the ensemble works? Does it pretty much date back to that?

Well it depends. If you’re playing with a clarinet and a trombone and you’re playing with guys that kind of come out of that tradition, I mean there’s certain roles that people tend to play. Like if I’m playing with Kenny Davern say and Dan Barrett, then like we’ll do that kind of playing where I stick fairly close to the lead, fairly close to the melody, improvising more on the melody. Kenny is playing above me, usually more notes, more obbligato, and Dan will be playing below, kind of like an embellished,…

items.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: We have Byron Stripling and Randy Sandke and Riley Mullins, a young fellow.

ctx.x: Who’s taking the trumpet part in that?

Well we have different people. We have Byron Stripling and Randy Sandke and Riley Mullins, a young fellow. And different people do it. We have Britt Woodman, Art Baron, Jerry Dodgion and Harry Allen. It’s quite exciting.
Amazing circle of musicians to choose from.
